dayTitle: What the plateau has been writing down
title: How thick a year is here
task: Turn a fortnight of snow into a year of record
scene: Brandt has the pit wall photographed and the last summer surface marked at 32 centimetres down. The snow above it weighs a third of what the same thickness of solid ice would.
question: Estimate this year's accumulation in ice equivalent.
takeaway: An accumulation rate means nothing until it is stated as the ice it will become.
why: Snow and ice are the same material at different densities, so a thickness of snow is not a thickness of record. Multiplying the layer by the ratio of the two densities converts it to the ice it will become once the air is squeezed out, which is the only form in which two sites can be compared. Vestri gets about 12 centimetres a year in ice equivalent. A coastal site gets a metre, and that difference decides everything downstream: how far back the core reaches, how thin the layers get, and how much older the ice is than its own trapped air.
assumes: snow becomes ice by being compressed under the snow that falls on it
answerText: About 0.12 metres of ice equivalent — a third of the snow thickness, because the snow is a third as dense.

estimate.prompt: The last summer surface sits 32 centimetres below this year's, in snow of density 340 kilograms per cubic metre.
estimate.question: Estimate this year's accumulation in metres of ice equivalent.
estimate.relationship: b = λ × ρ_snow ÷ ρ_ice — the snow layer λ scaled by the ratio of its own density to the density of solid ice.
estimate.explanation: The water density is the tile that does not belong: the conversion is snow to ice, and liquid water is never part of this record.

dayTitle: What the plateau has been writing down
title: Why the hole is on the dome
task: Say what the site was chosen for
scene: The drill engineer, Pär Lindqvist, has the hole at 2,040 metres and a map on the wall with 3 abandoned sites on it, all of them on slopes. Vestri Dome is the high point for 200 kilometres.
question: What does drilling at the dome buy that a site on the slope cannot?
takeaway: A core is a column of what fell above it only where the ice has not travelled sideways.
why: An ice sheet flows outwards from its high points. On a slope the ice at a given depth arrived from somewhere upstream, so a core there mixes the weather of one place with the history of a journey, and the two cannot be separated afterwards. Under a dome the flow is almost straight down, so the column below the drill is very nearly the snow that fell on it. Domes pay for that: they are high, cold and dry, which means thin layers and a long slow season.
assumes: ice spreads outwards from the high points of an ice sheet
answerText: The ice at each depth fell close to where it now sits, so the core is a column of one place's weather.

choices: The ice at each depth fell near this spot, not upstream
The ice is colder at the summit, which slows the chemical reactions in it
Snowfall is heaviest at the high point, giving the thickest annual layers
The bedrock beneath a dome is flattest, which keeps a three-kilometre hole vertical
rebuttals: Summit ice is colder, and cold ice is not what makes depth correspond to time
Domes are the driest part of an ice sheet, not the snowiest — thin layers are the price paid here
Bed shape matters to the deepest ice, and it is not why the site sits at the high point

dayTitle: What the plateau has been writing down
title: What makes one year different from the next
task: Read a year off the core
scene: A metre of core from 60 metres is on the light table. The chronology lead, Ines Okonkwo, has four features marked on it and wants each one attributed before the section is cut.
takeaway: A year is counted from several signals that agree, not from one that looks convincing.
why: No single marker survives the whole core, so a year is established where several independent signals line up. Coarse crystals form on a summer surface that stayed exposed; conductivity spikes are acid, and volcanic acid arrives in a season; dust is delivered by winds thousands of kilometres away and peaks with their season; the light and dark banding is bubble structure changing as each layer was compressed. Where three of the four agree, a year is a year. Where only one does, it is a candidate.
assumes: snow that falls in summer sits under different conditions from snow that falls in winter

choices: A summer surface that sat exposed and grew coarse before it was buried
Acid from an eruption, laid down in a season or two and then gone
Windier months on distant continents, carried here and settled out
Bubble size changing through the year as the snow was compressed
rebuttals: Conductivity responds to acid, and the coarse crystal band is a surface that was left exposed
Dust is delivered from elsewhere and does not follow the crystal growth on this surface
Banding tracks how the snow was compressed rather than what was carried in from outside
scenarios: A band of large, loosely bonded crystals
A narrow spike in electrical conductivity
A rise in fine mineral dust
Alternating light and dark bands about a centimetre apart

dayTitle: Three kilometres of one attempt
title: The run through the brittle zone
task: Bring a brittle section up whole
scene: The barrel is at 780 metres, inside the depth range where the ice comes up cracked. The winch, the fluid and the storage are all set for ordinary ice and Lindqvist wants the order settled before the lift starts.
takeaway: Ice recovered badly is a shorter record, not a cheaper one.
why: Between about 51200 metres the bubbles are at pressures the surface cannot support, and the ice around them fractures as it is brought up. Each step buys the next one: a slow lift reduces the shock, resting the core at hole temperature lets the pressure equalise gradually, logging the breaks fixes what depth each fragment came from before anything moves, and storing it for weeks lets it finish cracking. Cutting first destroys the depth information and cuts a section that is still moving.
assumes: gas trapped at depth is at the pressure of the ice around it

cards: Slow the winch through the depth band where bubbles are at their highest pressure
Let the section rest in the trench at drill-hole temperature before it is handled
Log the breaks and their positions before anything is moved off the barrel
Carry the section to the storage trench and leave it there for the relaxation period
Cut and distribute only after the section has stopped cracking

dayTitle: Three kilometres of one attempt
title: The metre with no label
task: Decide what an unmarked section is worth
scene: A section has arrived at the line with a broken depth mark. Holt can place it to within about four metres from the run sheet, and the isotope team has asked for it.
question: What should the section be used for?
takeaway: A sample without a depth is a measurement of nothing in particular.
why: A depth is what converts a measurement into a statement about a year. Four metres here is thirty-odd years, so an isotope value from this section cannot be placed in the record and would sit in it as a point with no time. It is still perfectly good ice for anything the depth does not enter: density, crystal fabric, how the drill is performing. The rule that matters is that the uncertainty travels with the sample, because the danger is not the gap — it is somebody downstream who never hears about it.
assumes: a measurement belongs to the depth it came from, and to no other
answerText: Work that does not need a precise depth — density, crystal fabric, drill performance — with the four-metre uncertainty recorded against it.

choices: Work that tolerates a four-metre depth uncertainty, recorded as such
Isotope work, since the four-metre window is small compared with the whole core
Nothing; an unplaced section is discarded so it cannot contaminate the record
Anything, once the run sheet is used to assign it the most likely depth
rebuttals: 4 metres is 30 years at this site, which is larger than most of the features the isotopes are used to find
Discarding it throws away measurements that never needed a depth in the first place
Assigning a most likely depth writes a guess into the record in the same handwriting as the measurements

equations.e: years = depth ÷ thickness of one year
equations.about: turning a depth into an age

dayTitle: Three kilometres of one attempt
title: The sample that was clean until it was handled
task: Find out where a signal came from
scene: The cold laboratory technician, Elena Cruz, has a sodium result four times higher than the run before it. She has the blank, the run order and the section's handling record on the bench.
takeaway: A blank measures the process, so anything it shows was never evidence about the ice.
why: The blank before the sample is ordinary and the blank after it is high, which places the contamination inside the run rather than in the ice. The trim was done to specification, so the outside of the section is ruled out, and the replicate core holds the same year with no sodium in it, so the atmosphere is ruled out as well. Every clean reading here is doing work: what identifies the source is not the loud number but which of the quiet ones stayed quiet.
assumes: a blank is run through the same process as a sample, with no sample in it

choices: Sea salt reached the plateau in the year this ice fell
Something in the laboratory entered the run and stayed
The outer surface was not trimmed
The replicate core missed the layer and is the wrong comparison
choiceMechanisms: A storm carried marine air far inland and the ice recorded it.
The process itself contributed, and went on contributing to what followed.
Drill fluid and handling left salt on the outside of the section.
The second hole missed the layer entirely.
text.headline: One sodium result is four times the run before it — and the blank that followed it is high too.

dayTitle: Counting to 2000
title: The depth the counting runs out
task: Find where the layers stop being countable
scene: The layer-thickness log runs from the surface to the bottom of the drilled core. The line can separate two bands three millimetres apart and no closer, and Okonkwo needs to know where the ice crosses that.
question: The line resolves bands three millimetres apart and no closer. At what depth does the annual layer thickness fall to that limit?
takeaway: A count ends where the instrument stops separating one year from the next.
why: Ice spreads outwards under its own weight, so every layer is stretched thinner as it sinks, and the thinning compounds with depth. At Vestri the surface lays down about 12 centimetres a year in ice equivalent; 2 kilometres down the same year is a few millimetres. Where the layers close to within the resolution of the measurement, the count stops — not because the years are gone, but because two of them can no longer be told apart. Everything deeper is dated by a flow model anchored to whatever dated events can still be found.
assumes: layers are stretched thinner as the ice below them spreads outwards
answerText: About 2,180 metres. Below that the bands are closer together than the line can separate, and the ages have to come from the flow model.

equations.e: years = depth ÷ thickness of one year
equations.about: turning a depth into an age

dayTitle: Counting to 2000
title: Which year marker survives the depth
task: Choose the signal to count with
scene: The isotope chemist, Yuki Tanabe, has 4 annual signals measured on the same stretch of core at 1,400 metres, where a year is about 26 millimetres thick.
question: At 1,400 metres, which signal is still able to separate 1 year from the next?
takeaway: A signal is only useful for counting while it is still sharper than the layer it marks.
why: Water molecules move through the open pores of the firn for decades. That movement smooths the isotope record. Anything thinner than about twice the diffusion length is averaged away, and at this site that removes the yearly signal long before 1,400 metres. Sodium arrives as sea salt. Dust arrives as mineral grains. Neither travels through the pore space, so their yearly structure survives as far down as the measurement can read it. Visible layering fades once the bubbles are gone, and conductivity marks eruptions.
assumes: water molecules can move through the connected air spaces in firn
answerText: The chemistry — sodium and dust — because those travel in the ice as particles and solutes rather than as water molecules, so firn diffusion never smoothed them.

choices: Sodium and dust, which never moved through the firn
The isotope ratio, which has the largest annual swing at the surface
Visible layering, which needs no chemical measurement to read at all
Electrical conductivity, which responds to every acid in the ice
rebuttals: The isotope swing is the largest at the surface and the first one diffusion removes
Visible banding depends on bubbles, which are gone below the depth where they turn to clathrate
Conductivity finds acid, and acid arrives when a volcano erupts rather than every year

equations.about: the mean of several years, or several samples

dayTitle: Counting to 2000
title: How old the bottom of the firn is
task: Put a number on the firn's own clock
scene: Brandt has the firn temperature string reading down to 88 metres, which is where the pores seal at this site. The surface is adding about 0.32 metres of snow a year.
question: Estimate the age of the snow at the close-off depth.
takeaway: A depth becomes an age only through the rate that filled it.
why: A depth–age scale is arithmetic on layer thicknesses: divide the depth by the thickness one year adds and you have the years it took to get there. In the firn the layers have not yet been thinned by flow, so the sum is a straight division; deeper in the ice the same calculation has to be done interval by interval as the layers get thinner. Nearly three centuries of snow sit above the close-off depth at Vestri, and every one of those years is still open to the atmosphere.
assumes: a depth divided by an annual layer thickness gives a number of years
answerText: About 275 years. The firn column here holds nearly three centuries of snow that has not yet become ice.

estimate.prompt: The pores seal at 88 metres. The surface adds about 0.32 metres of snow a year, and the firn has not been thinned by flow.
estimate.question: Estimate the age of the snow at the close-off depth.
estimate.relationship: age = depth ÷ annual layer thickness, valid while the layers have not yet been thinned by ice flow.
estimate.explanation: The ice-equivalent figure is the distractor: the firn is snow, and this depth is measured in snow.
labels: 0.119 m/yr  (the same year in ice equivalent)

equations.e: years = depth ÷ thickness of one year
equations.about: turning a depth into an age

dayTitle: Turning a ratio into a temperature
title: What the ratio says in degrees
task: Put the profile into degrees
scene: Tanabe has the isotope profile against depth, and the section covering the last cold interval sits 1.8 per mil below the modern surface value. The site's calibration slope is on the board.
question: Estimate the temperature change that isotope shift represents.
takeaway: A slope converts a measurement into a claim, and it is measured rather than assumed.
why: Water carrying the heavy isotope condenses first. Air that has cooled further has already lost more of it, so the snow falling last is the lightest. Over a useful range the ratio and the temperature move together in a straight line. The slope of that line is not a constant of physics. It belongs to this site's weather, and it is measured by comparing the isotope record with the mast during the years that have both. Dividing the shift by the slope gives the change in degrees.
assumes: colder air loses its heavier water molecules earlier, leaving the snow isotopically lighter
answerText: About 2.7 degrees colder. The shift is 1.8 per mil and the site slope is 0.67 per mil for every degree.

estimate.prompt: The cold interval sits 1.8 per mil below the modern surface value. Calibration against the mast gives 0.67 per mil for each degree of temperature change.
estimate.question: Estimate the temperature difference between that interval and the present.
estimate.relationship: ΔT = Δδ¹⁸O ÷ α — the isotope shift in parts per thousand, divided by the site's calibration slope in parts per thousand per degree.
estimate.explanation: The deuterium slope belongs to a different isotope of a different element, and using it here would give an answer 11 times too small.

equations.e: years = depth ÷ thickness of one year
equations.about: turning a depth into an age

dayTitle: Turning a ratio into a temperature
title: How firmly the cooling can be stated
task: State the cooling with its uncertainty
scene: Brandt has the mast record, the calibration years and the scatter around the fitted slope. The season summary needs a statement that the interval was colder than the present, and how sure of it anybody is.
question: Which work would let the summary state that the interval was more than two degrees colder?
takeaway: Narrowing a distribution and moving it are different actions with different evidence behind them.
why: The reconstruction is a distribution, not a number: the slope was fitted to 11 years of overlap and it carries the scatter of that fit. A claim that the interval was more than two degrees colder is a claim about where the whole distribution sits, so it is cleared by making the distribution narrower rather than by moving its middle. More overlap years is the only action here that adds information; the source-region correction changes the central value and leaves the spread exactly as wide as it was.
assumes: a fitted relationship carries a spread as well as a central value
answerText: Extending the overlap with the mast record. It narrows the calibration spread, which is what the claim needs; re-centring the slope moves the estimate without making it any surer.

equations.e: years = depth ÷ thickness of one year
equations.about: turning a depth into an age

dayTitle: Turning a ratio into a temperature
title: The temperature of what, and where
task: Say what the thermometer is a thermometer of
scene: Aalto is drafting the summary line and has written that the isotopes give the temperature of the last cold interval. Halvorsen wants the sentence narrowed before it goes anywhere.
question: What does the isotope record most directly record?
takeaway: A proxy measures one specific thing, and the sentence has to say which.
why: The isotope ratio is set as water vapour condenses, so it records conditions in the cloud that produced this snow, weighted towards the seasons that deliver most of it. Getting from there to a surface temperature needs the relationship between cloud and ground, which is what the site calibration supplies. The ocean the water came from does leave a mark, which is why source-region corrections exist. The ice's own temperature is a separate measurement, taken with a thermometer in the borehole, and it says nothing about the year the snow fell.
assumes: snow forms in a cloud and falls to a surface some distance below it
answerText: The condensation temperature of the air that made this snow, which is close to but not the same as the surface temperature here.

choices: Where the snow condensed, over this region, in the season it fell
The average annual temperature of the whole hemisphere at that time
The temperature of the ice itself, preserved from when it was buried
The temperature of the ocean the water evaporated from
rebuttals: A single site records its own region; hemispheric averages are built by combining many sites
Borehole thermometry measures the ice now, and is used to check the isotopes rather than to replace them
Evaporation conditions leave a second-order mark, which is a correction rather than the signal

dayTitle: Air that stopped moving
title: How much younger the air is
task: Put a number on the age offset
scene: The pores seal at 88 metres here. Above that the firn is open to the atmosphere, and its mean density is about 0.62 of solid ice. Adeyemi has the accumulation rate on the board beside it.
question: Estimate the age difference between a bubble and the ice around it.
takeaway: A bubble is sealed at a depth, and the ice around it arrived at that depth long before.
why: Air circulates through the connected pore spaces of the firn and mixes with the atmosphere until those pores close, so the air in a bubble is roughly as old as the moment of sealing while the ice around it is as old as the snow. Converting the firn column to ice equivalent and dividing by the accumulation rate gives that interval. It is set by how deep the close-off is and how fast snow arrives, so cold dry sites carry offsets of centuries and wet coastal ones a few decades. Ignore it and a gas record is plotted centuries too early.
assumes: air moves freely through connected pore spaces until they close
answerText: About 460 years. The snow at close-off depth is that old, and the air sealed into it is essentially modern at the moment of sealing.

estimate.prompt: Close-off is at 88 metres, the firn above it averages 0.62 of the density of solid ice, and the site accumulates 0.119 metres of ice equivalent a year.
estimate.question: Estimate the difference between the age of the gas and the age of the ice around it.
estimate.relationship: Δage ≈ z_close × ρ̄ ÷ b — the close-off depth, scaled by mean firn density, divided by the accumulation in ice equivalent.
estimate.explanation: The snow thickness is the distractor: the density conversion has already been applied, so using it again would count the same correction twice.
labels: 0.32 m/yr  (the same year as a snow thickness)

equations.about: how fast the drill is going down

equations.e: years = depth ÷ thickness of one year
equations.about: turning a depth into an age

dayTitle: Air that stopped moving
title: From snowfall to sealed bubble
task: Name the step that fixes the offset
scene: Lindqvist has the borehole's own record on the wall: five stages between a snowflake landing and air being locked away, with a measurement against each one.
question: Which stage decides how much older the ice is than the air inside it?
takeaway: In a chain of stages, one of them sets the answer and the others follow it.
why: Every stage moves something, but only one of them fixes the size of the offset. Air exchanges with the atmosphere all the way down the firn, so its age barely changes while the ice around it gets older year by year; the moment the pores seal is the moment that exchange stops, and the age difference is fixed at whatever the ice's age is at that depth. Mixing looks like the answer because it is the process that keeps the air young, but its effect is a decade against a difference of centuries.
assumes: a quantity that passes through several stages is limited by one of them
answerText: Pore close-off. The offset is the age of the ice at the depth where the pores seal, so everything above that depth is a firn column and everything below it is a bubble.

dayTitle: Air that stopped moving
title: Why the gas record has no sharp edges
task: Explain the smoother record
scene: Okonkwo has the two records from the same depths on one plot. The ice record has features a few years wide. The gas record from the same interval has nothing narrower than a few decades.
question: Why is the gas record smoother than the ice record from the same depths?
takeaway: A record made by an averaging process cannot show a change faster than the averaging.
why: Air is in contact with the atmosphere throughout the open firn, and the pores do not all close at once — the closing happens across a depth range, so the bubbles sealed in one layer hold a mixture spanning the years that range represents. That smoothing is a property of the site: a high-accumulation site closes its pores in a decade and keeps sharp features, while this one takes several. Sample size makes a small contribution and could be reduced by cutting smaller pieces. The smoothing cannot.
assumes: a measurement that averages over an interval cannot show anything shorter than it
answerText: The air mixed through the whole firn column before it was sealed, so each bubble holds an average of several decades of atmosphere rather than one year of it.

choices: Each bubble holds air mixed over the decades it took the pores to close
Gas measurements are made on larger samples, so they average more ice
Carbon dioxide changes more slowly in the atmosphere than temperature does
Bubbles leak slowly into one another over thousands of years
rebuttals: Sample size is a choice and could be made smaller; the firn smoothing is fixed by the site
Some atmospheric changes are genuinely fast, and this record could not show them either
Bubbles are sealed and do not exchange with each other on any timescale that matters here

equations.e: years = depth ÷ thickness of one year
equations.about: turning a depth into an age

dayTitle: The year that is written everywhere
title: The spike at 1,642 metres
task: Identify the horizon
scene: One sulphate spike, two candidate eruptions of similar age, and a set of glass shards recovered from the same centimetre. Okonkwo has the shard chemistry, the layer count and the modelled age on the bench.
takeaway: A horizon is identified by what is in it, not by the date it would be convenient for it to have.
why: The shard chemistry is the only reading here that is independent of the timescale, and it is the one that discriminates: glass composition is a fingerprint of a particular magma and a particular volcano. The modelled age cannot choose between 2 candidates 90 years apart because its own uncertainty is larger than that gap. Sea-salt sulphate does not arrive with volcanic glass. And waiting for the layer count is waiting for something that stopped 460 metres higher, which is the reason a dated horizon matters here at all.
assumes: volcanic glass carries the chemical composition of the volcano that erupted it

choices: The northern eruption, identified by the shard chemistry
The southern eruption, since the modelled age fits it slightly better
Neither; the spike is a sea-salt sulphate peak
Undecidable until the layer count is extended down to it
choiceMechanisms: Glass composition is specific to a volcano and does not depend on the timescale.
The flow model puts this depth marginally closer to the southern date.
Marine sulphate can produce peaks without any volcano at all.
Nothing can be assigned a date without a continuous count reaching it.
text.headline: A sulphate spike at 1,642 m, with glass shards, and 2 candidate eruptions within a century of each other.

equations.e: years = depth ÷ thickness of one year
equations.about: turning a depth into an age

dayTitle: The year that is written everywhere
title: What a dated ash layer fixes
task: Say what the tie point does for the gas
scene: Adeyemi has the eruption date, the depth it sits at, and the carbon dioxide measurements from the bubbles in the same section of core.
question: What does the dated horizon fix?
takeaway: A tie point dates the material it is in, and anything else has to be reached by a calculation.
why: Ash falls onto the surface and is buried with the snow, so it dates the ice it sits in. The air in the bubbles beside it was sealed centuries later, at the close-off depth, and it is that much younger. A tie point therefore fixes one of the two clocks in the core and leaves the other one to be reached by calculation — which is exactly why the age difference has to be estimated before any comparison between a gas record and an ice record can be made.
assumes: volcanic ash settles out of the atmosphere within a year or two of an eruption
answerText: The age of the ice at that depth. The age of the gas in the same section still has to be reached by subtracting the age difference.

choices: The age of the ice at that depth, and nothing else on its own
The age of both the ice and the gas at that depth, since they are in the same section
The age of the gas, because the ash and the atmosphere arrived together
The accumulation rate at that time, from the thickness of the ash layer
rebuttals: The two clocks are in the same section and are not the same clock, which is what the age difference measures
Ash arrives at the surface, and the air at that depth stopped moving centuries after it was buried
A layer thickness gives an accumulation rate only once its own age scale is known

dayTitle: The year that is written everywhere
title: One clear day, three jobs
task: Spend the clear day
scene: Brandt has a forecast that gives her one clear day and then four of blowing snow. Three jobs are outstanding and each takes most of a day on its own.
question: Which job takes the clear day?
takeaway: Order the work by what becomes impossible, not by what is most important.
why: Two of these can be done in bad weather and one cannot. The pit is beside the hut and the mast is a short walk on a fixed line, so both survive four days of blowing snow with nothing worse than discomfort. The stake array runs two kilometres out and needs visibility to level against; more to the point, blowing snow redistributes the surface the stakes are measuring, so a reading taken after the storm is measuring something different. The shallow core can be re-drilled in any weather at all.
assumes: a measurement that cannot be repeated should be taken when it can be taken
answerText: The stake farm. It is the only one of the three that cannot be done in blowing snow, and a missed reading is a gap in the accumulation series that nothing can fill later.

choices: Read and re-level the stake farm across the whole array
Dig and photograph the fortnightly snow pit beside the hut
Service the mast instruments and download the temperature record
Re-drill the shallow firn core that broke last week
rebuttals: The pit is a few metres from the hut door and can be dug in any weather
The mast is on a fixed line and its record is stored until somebody collects it
A firn core that broke can be re-drilled whenever the drill is free

dayTitle: Two records, side by side
title: What both records rest on
task: Find what the two records share
scene: Five pieces of the comparison are on Aalto's screen, each one computed from something. Okonkwo wants to know which of them would still stand if the flow model were wrong.
question: Which parts of this comparison would survive the flow model being wrong?
takeaway: Two numbers that agree because they came through the same step have not confirmed each other.
why: Both groups counted layers as far as they could and then handed the rest to the same flow model, with the same assumption of uniform vertical strain. Below those counts the two age scales are not independent estimates that happen to agree; they are one calculation applied twice. What survives the model being wrong is the counted section, which is arithmetic on measured layers, and the tephra horizon, whose date came from a volcano and not from any ice. Those two are the comparison. The rest is a shared assumption.
assumes: two results computed from one assumption fail together if that assumption fails
answerText: The counted section and the tephra tie point. Everything below the counts on both sides was dated with the same flow model, so those two agreeing establishes nothing about it.

dayTitle: Two records, side by side
title: What the carbon dioxide change was worth
task: Turn a gas record into an energy number
scene: Adeyemi has carbon dioxide at 190 parts per million through the cold interval and 280 at the top of the core. Halvorsen wants the difference expressed as an energy imbalance.
question: Estimate the radiative forcing between the two concentrations.
takeaway: A concentration becomes a climate statement only through the energy it changes.
why: Carbon dioxide absorbs in bands that are already partly saturated, so each extra molecule does less than the one before it, and the forcing goes as the logarithm of the concentration rather than in proportion to it. That is why the effect is usually stated per doubling: every doubling adds about the same. Between the cold interval and the top of the core the concentration rose by half, which is worth about two watts on every square metre of the planet, sustained for as long as it lasts.
assumes: a greenhouse gas reduces the rate at which the surface loses heat to space
answerText: About 2.1 watts per square metre. The change from 190 to 280 parts per million is roughly a third of the way to a doubling.

estimate.prompt: Carbon dioxide is 190 parts per million in the cold interval and 280 at the top of the core.
estimate.question: Estimate the radiative forcing between the two.
estimate.relationship: ΔF = 5.35 × ln(C ÷ C₀) — the logarithm of the concentration ratio, times the coefficient for carbon dioxide, in watts per square metre.
estimate.explanation: The isotope slope converts a ratio into degrees at this site, which is a different step in a different part of the argument.

dayTitle: Two records, side by side
title: Half a per mil, in degrees
task: Say what the offset is worth in degrees
scene: The two records differ by about half a per mil through the cold interval. Tanabe has the site calibration slope and Halvorsen's draft paragraph, which calls the difference a different climate.
question: What does half a per mil amount to, in the terms the draft paragraph uses?
takeaway: A difference has to be converted into the units of the claim before anybody can judge it.
why: The site slope is 0.67 per mil for each degree, so half a per mil is about 0.75 of a degree. That is the whole point of converting: in per mil the difference sounds like a rounding error, and in degrees it is a quarter of the cooling the season intends to report. Whether it is a real climate difference or a shared method's shortcoming is a separate question, and it cannot be argued about honestly until both sides are talking in the same units.
assumes: an isotope difference is converted to a temperature difference by the site slope
answerText: About three quarters of a degree — which is smaller than the cooling being reported and large enough to matter to it.

choices: About three quarters of a degree — a quarter of the reported cooling
About half a degree, since the slope is close to one per mil for each degree
Nothing until the difference exceeds the scatter of a single measurement
About four degrees, since the slope is measured in per mil per degree
rebuttals: A slope of one per mil per degree is not this site's slope, and using it changes the answer by half
Scatter on a single measurement is much smaller than this difference, which is why it was noticed
Multiplying by the slope instead of dividing by it gives a number about 5 times too large

dayTitle: The offset that was not climate
title: What the correction leaves behind
task: Predict, correct, then check
scene: Adeyemi has the age difference for both sites and the machinery to re-plot both gas records on their own gas timescales. The tephra horizon is dated independently of either calculation.
question: What is left of the difference once both gas records are on their own gas timescales?
takeaway: A prediction made before the correction is the only thing that can test it.
why: Air keeps mixing with the atmosphere until the firn seals, so gas is younger than the ice around it by an amount set by how deep the sealing is and how fast snow arrives. Skarv accumulates four times as fast, so its offset is a fraction of this station's. Plotting both gas records on ice timescales therefore shifts one curve much further than the other, and produces a difference that looks like climate and is arithmetic. What makes the corrected answer trustworthy is the tephra: a date neither calculation produced.
assumes: a correction should be predicted before it is applied, or it cannot be wrong
answerText: About 0.15 per mil — most of the difference was the age offset, and what remains is inside both groups' stated uncertainties.

equations.about: how fast the drill is going down

dayTitle: The offset that was not climate
title: The clock that does not need layers
task: Date ice the counting cannot reach
scene: Okonkwo has a sample from the deep section and a radiometric result: the isotope in it has fallen to 0.55 of the amount it starts with. Its mean lifetime is on the bench.
question: Estimate the age of the sample from what is left of the isotope.
takeaway: Where counting has run out, a clock that runs on its own is the only independent date left.
why: Radioactive decay proceeds at a rate that no temperature, pressure or flow in the ice can change, which is what makes it usable where the layers have stopped being countable. The amount left falls exponentially with time, so taking the natural logarithm of the fraction remaining and multiplying by the mean lifetime gives the age directly. It carries its own uncertainties — how much was there to begin with, whether anything was added or lost — and none of them is the flow model, which is why the result is worth having.
assumes: a radioactive isotope decays at a rate nothing in the ice can change
answerText: About 4,900 years. Decay is the one clock in the core that does not depend on the flow model.

estimate.prompt: The isotope has fallen to 0.55 of its initial amount. Its mean lifetime is 8,267 years.
estimate.question: Estimate the age of the sample.
estimate.relationship: t = −τ × ln(N ÷ N₀) — the isotope's mean lifetime, times the logarithm of the fraction still remaining.
estimate.explanation: The half-life is the same clock in different units and belongs in a different form of the equation; using it here gives an age a third too short.
labels: 5730 yr  (the half-life of the same isotope)

equations.e: years = depth ÷ thickness of one year
equations.about: turning a depth into an age

dayTitle: The offset that was not climate
title: What is left to disagree about
task: Say what the corrected comparison supports
scene: Both records are re-plotted, the tephra horizon lines up in both, and 0.15 per mil of difference remains. Both groups quote uncertainties larger than that.
question: What does the corrected comparison support?
takeaway: Explaining a disagreement away is a result, and it is the result that has to be published.
why: What remains after the correction is smaller than either group's stated uncertainty, so there is no measured difference left to explain. That is a positive result rather than an absence of one: two independently drilled cores, once put on comparable clocks, record the same cooling. The correction does not weaken it — it was predicted before it was applied and then checked against a date that came from neither calculation. And nothing here makes Skarv wrong; both records were plotted on the wrong clock, and only one of them moved far.
assumes: a difference smaller than the uncertainty of either measurement is not a measured difference
answerText: That the two records are consistent, and that most of the apparent difference was the gas–ice age offset rather than climate.

choices: The two records are consistent once both are on gas timescales
The two records disagree, but by less than was first thought
Nothing at all, since a correction had to be applied to reach the result
The Skarv record is wrong, since its offset was the smaller of the two
rebuttals: A remaining difference below both uncertainties is not a disagreement of any size
A correction that was predicted and then tested is evidence rather than a weakness
Both records were on ice timescales; the offset is smaller at Skarv because it snows more there

dayTitle: The night the generator stopped
title: Six signatures and two hours
task: Check what is worth checking
scene: Six lines on the night sheet, all signed. Tanabe has two hours before the flight manifest closes and can verify two of them properly.
question: Which two claims should the two hours verify?
takeaway: A signed record is evidence that a claim was made, which is not evidence that it was true.
why: A signature says that somebody believed something when they signed, and the store reading of minus 19 says the belief was wrong for at least part of the night. Two of these claims are both critical and carried by nothing but the signature — the store and the gas samples — and both decide whether measurements made on that ice can be defended. The mast is critical and already carries its own continuous record; the drill tank has an independent logger. The food and the fuel matter to the camp and not to the science.
assumes: a signature records that somebody believed something, at the time they signed
answerText: The store temperature and the gas samples. Both are critical, both are signed with nothing behind them, and both would invalidate measurements if they are wrong.

dayTitle: The night the generator stopped
title: What comes back first
task: Put the restart in order
scene: Power is back on one generator. Lindqvist, de Vries and Tanabe each want their own system restarted first, and the single generator will not carry all of them at once.
question: What is restarted first?
takeaway: Restart in the order of what is still being lost, not in the order of who asked.
why: Three of these are waiting and one is deteriorating. Ice above minus 20 starts losing gas from the bubbles near its cut faces, and that loss cannot be undone or measured around; every hour is more of the core that can no longer answer a gas question. A lost drilling day is a day, the queued samples are as good tomorrow as today, and a report sent six hours late is a report sent. Order by what is still being lost.
assumes: a system that has already failed is more informative than one that has not yet been used
answerText: The core store. It is the only 1 of the 4 still losing something irreversibly, and every hour above minus 20 costs gas measurements that cannot be made again.

choices: The core store refrigeration, which is still warming
The drill, so the day's run is not lost
The chemistry line, so the 16 queued samples can be run
The satellite link, so the season report can be sent
rebuttals: A drilling day is recoverable, and the drill is not losing anything while it stands idle
Queued samples are in the store; if the store is warm they are the thing being lost, not the queue
A report is not perishable, and the link is the only item here that changes nothing by waiting

dayTitle: The night the generator stopped
title: How much of it is noise
task: Say how tightly the mean can be quoted
scene: Aalto has 30 years of reconstructed annual temperature from the top of the core. The year-to-year scatter is 1.4 degrees and the summary wants a mean for the period.
question: Estimate the standard error of the thirty-year mean.
takeaway: An average is only as tight as the scatter divided by the root of how many years went into it.
why: Individual years scatter because weather scatters, and averaging does not remove that scatter — it reduces the uncertainty of the average, and only as the square root of the number of years. 30 years of a record with 1.4 degrees of year-to-year variation give a mean known to about a quarter of a degree. Two such means half a degree apart are two standard errors apart, which is where a claim of difference starts becoming defensible and not before. Doubling the precision would take 120 years.
assumes: averaging independent years reduces the scatter of the average, not of the years
answerText: About 0.26 degrees. A difference between two such means smaller than half a degree is not a difference at all.

estimate.prompt: The reconstructed annual temperatures scatter by 1.4 degrees, and the period is 30 years long.
estimate.question: Estimate the standard error of the thirty-year mean.
estimate.relationship: SE = s ÷ √n — the year-to-year scatter, divided by the square root of how many years were averaged.
estimate.explanation: The calibration slope is already inside the reconstruction; applying it again would convert degrees into degrees per degree.

equations.e: years = depth ÷ thickness of one year
equations.about: turning a depth into an age
the mean of several years, or several samples

dayTitle: What is known, and how well
title: The sentence the record will carry
task: Choose the sentence the record supports
scene: Four versions of the season's headline claim, all of them true in some sense, on Aalto's screen. One of them is the one the evidence actually reaches.
question: Which sentence does this season's evidence reach?
takeaway: An honest claim states what was measured, over what period, with what uncertainty.
why: The first sentence says what was measured, over what interval, and which part of it depends on something that was not measured here. The second calls the two records independent, which the shared flow model makes untrue below the counts. The third rounds the number until the uncertainty disappears into it and attributes agreement to a site whose comparison needed a correction. The fourth is a claim about every other record at this latitude, and nobody at this station has read them all.
assumes: a claim is supported when the evidence would have come out differently if it were false
answerText: The one that names the cooling, the period, the uncertainty and the fact that the deep dating rests on a flow model.

choices: A cooling of about 2.7 degrees, modelled below the counted section
A cooling of 2.7 degrees, established by 2 independent records
A cooling of about three degrees, consistent with the Skarv site
The largest cooling yet recorded at this latitude, pending the deep section
rebuttals: The two records share a flow model below their counts, so "independent" is the word that fails
Rounding to three degrees hides the uncertainty that decides whether this differs from other sites
A superlative is a claim about everybody else's records, which this season did not examine

dayTitle: What is known, and how well
title: What rests on what
task: Sort established from assumed
scene: Brandt has the season's four headline numbers written on the hut wall and a column beside each one that nobody has filled in.
takeaway: Every number in a proxy record belongs to a class, and the class is part of the number.
why: The four numbers are not the same kind of thing, and the report has to say so. The accumulation is a direct measurement of the surface and can be checked next year. The cooling is a measurement passed through a calibration, so it inherits the calibration's uncertainty. The age is counted where counting worked and modelled where it did not. The gas concentration is a solid measurement of a global quantity attached to a depth whose age is itself modelled — strong in what it measures, weaker in when it happened.
assumes: a number is only as strong as the weakest step between the ice and it

choices: Measured directly at the surface, and checkable against next season's stakes
Measured, then converted through a slope fitted to 11 years of overlap
Counted as far as the layers allowed, and modelled below that
Measured on air that is well mixed, at a depth whose own age is modelled
rebuttals: The cooling is not a direct surface measurement; it arrives through a fitted slope
The age below the counted section is not checkable against next season's stakes
The gas concentration is well measured and its date is the modelled part of it
scenarios: Accumulation of 0.119 metres of ice equivalent a year
A cooling of 2.7 degrees in the cold interval
An age of 18,400 years at 2,100 metres
Carbon dioxide of 190 parts per million in the cold interval

dayTitle: What is known, and how well
title: The shortest thing this ice can show
task: Put a number on the finest event
scene: Tanabe has the firn diffusion length for this site and the surface layer thickness. The next team wants to know whether a single warm summer could ever be found in this core.
question: Estimate the shortest event this record could still resolve, in years.
takeaway: A record has a shortest event it can show, and it is set by the site rather than by the instrument.
why: Water molecules diffuse through the connected pores of the firn for as long as those pores are open, which averages each layer with its neighbours. The scale of that averaging is the diffusion length, and anything thinner than about twice it is smoothed away past recovery. Dividing that limit by the annual layer thickness gives the answer in years. At the surface this site can just about hold a single year; deeper, where the layers have thinned, the same diffusion length covers many years and the annual signal is gone for good.
assumes: water molecules move through firn before the pores seal, averaging nearby layers together
answerText: About 1.3 years at the surface, and longer at every depth below it as the layers thin.

estimate.prompt: The firn diffusion length at this site is 0.08 metres, and a year at the surface is 0.119 metres of ice equivalent.
estimate.question: Estimate the shortest event the isotope record could still resolve.
estimate.relationship: shortest event = 2σ ÷ λ — twice the diffusion length, divided by the thickness of 1 annual layer.
estimate.explanation: Using the deep layer thickness instead would answer a different question — the resolution at 2,400 metres, which is nearly 7 years.
labels: 2  (the factor below which a feature is lost)

equations.e: years = depth ÷ thickness of one year
equations.about: turning a depth into an age
